intro_html: One trip into the oil at 175 °C, after simmering and drying the potatoes. A dry tempura mix sold for shrimp works for vegetables too: use its packet water ratio. This herb seasoning is a fusion variation. For a potato-only crust and two fries, see crispy twice-fried wedges. This is a source-informed home adaptation, not a kitchen-tested recipe.

items: peeled; cut lengthwise, 15 mm at the thickest part

mise.name: Potato wedges

notes.html:
• Instead of the packet mix and its water, use 80 g plain flour + 20 g cornstarch + 150 ml ice-cold sparkling water.
  • Stir briefly with a fork, leaving a few small lumps.
  • No egg needed.
  • Keep the separate 15 g dusting cornstarch.
  • This is an alternative batter, not an addition to the packet mix.

• Tempura mix is uncooked powder that becomes batter with water.
  • Tenkasu/agedama are already-fried batter bits: sprinkle a spoonful on the finished dish if you like; frying them again can burn them.
  • Panko are breadcrumbs for a different breaded coating.
  • If your package says shrimp tempura batter mix, use it here.
notes.title_html: Tempura mix, tempura bits or panko?

notes.html:
• A raw 15 mm wedge can stay hard inside while tempura browns.
  • Simmering first separates those jobs: the potato becomes tender, then frying cooks the thin shell and reheats the centre.
  • A second hot fry is useful for bare potato crust, but this thin batter shell is ready after one fry.
  • For raw potato tempura, use a separate recipe for thin 5 mm slices.
notes.title_html: Why precook and only fry once?

notes.html:
• Coating slips off: the potato was wet, the starch layer was too thick, or the batter was too runny.
  • Pat the potato dry, leave only a faint starch film and let excess batter drip off.
  • Heavy or greasy coating: keep the batter cold, avoid overmixing and restore the oil temperature between small batches.
  • The homemade batter quantities in the note are for the original 500 g potato batch; multiply them by the same factor as the potatoes when changing servings.
notes.title_html: A thin shell that sticks to the potato

steps.body_html:
• Use Russet, Maris Piper, King Edward or another floury frying potato. Peel and cut lengthwise into 6 wedges per medium potato; cut a large one into 8. Aim for 15 mm at the thickest part, not a fixed number of pieces. Split any wedge wider than 20 mm. Rinse once.
  • Bring the water and simmering salt to a boil. Add the wedges, return to a gentle simmer, then cook about 7–10 minutes. Start checking at 6 minutes: a thin knife should enter the thickest centre easily, while the wedge still lifts intact. Tenderness decides when to drain.
  • Do not add baking soda and do not roughen these wedges: an intact surface holds the thin batter better.
steps.title: Cut and simmer the wedges

steps.body_html: • Drain gently and spread apart on a rack. Let steam escape for 10 minutes, then refrigerate uncovered about 20 minutes, until cool and surface-dry. Pat away any remaining droplets. Prepare the finishing seasoning while they cool.
steps.title: Cool and dry thoroughly

steps.body_html:
• Use refined sunflower, rapeseed/canola or peanut oil. In an electric fryer follow its minimum and maximum fill lines. In a pot use about 5 cm depth and fill no more than one third. Fry roughly 150–200 g at a time in a 3-litre fryer, less in a small pot; wedges need room. Restore the stated temperature between batches. Surface water must be gone before any potato enters oil.
  • Heat oil to 175 °C. Prepare 100 g dry tempura mix with ice-cold water in the packet ratio, including egg only if the packet requires it. Keep the bowl over ice, with ice outside the batter. Mix as the packet directs and use promptly; the coating should run off a spoon in a thin film.
  • Dust only a few dry wedges lightly with cornstarch, tap off excess, then dip in batter and let excess drip. Coat each batch immediately before frying. Do not bread with dry tempura mix or add cooked tempura crumbs to the batter.

steps.body_html:
• Lower 3–5 wedges individually into the oil, without touching. In an electric fryer lower the empty basket first, then add battered wedges according to its instructions so the wet coating does not glue itself around the mesh.
  • Maintain 170–175 °C while frying for about 4–5 minutes, turning once, until the thin shell is crisp and pale gold and the potato is hot through. Open one thick wedge to check. Skim loose batter and restore 175 °C before the next batch. There is no second fry in this version.

steps.body_html: • Drain on a rack for 30–60 seconds. Sprinkle with the mixed salt, oregano, basil, garlic powder and pepper while hot, tasting before adding it all. Serve immediately, without covering or piling up, with optional mayonnaise on the side.
